summary: For ages 7-8, learners draw picture graphs (one symbol = one unit) and bar graphs (labelled axes, single-unit scale) with up to four categories, then use the finished graph to solve put-together, take-apart and compare ('how many more') problems. The core skill is translating both ways: from organised counts to a scaled visual, and from the visual back to a count that answers a question. Teaching builds the graph from the children's own data, insists on equal-width bars rising from a common baseline read against the scale, and models 'how many more' as the difference (the gap) between two bars rather than the taller bar's value.
misconceptions: Answers 'how many more' with the taller bar's value instead of the difference between the bars
Reads a bar's value off by one (counts gridlines instead of the value the top reaches, or bars not starting at zero)
Draws bars of unequal width, floating off the baseline, or unevenly spaced, so height no longer means count
Draws picture-graph symbols of different sizes or unaligned, so rows can't be compared by length

activities.title: Build a bar graph from our data on gridded paper
steps: Collect or use a given data set with up to four categories (e.g. favourite pets: cats 9, dogs 6, fish 4, birds 2)
On squared/gridded paper or a gridded canvas, draw one bar per category, shading one square per unit so each bar's height equals its count
Keep every bar the same width, rising from a common baseline (zero line), evenly spaced, and label both axes with a single-unit scale
Read a chosen bar's value back by tracking its top straight across to the scale number, and check it matches the original count
activities.insight: Height means count: a bar's top read against the scale gives the number of items in that category. This only works if every bar starts from the shared zero baseline. Equal widths keep the bars fair to compare by eye, so that only height carries the count.

activities.title: 'How many more' as the gap between two bars
steps: On a finished bar graph, pick two categories and state a comparison question, e.g. 'how many more children chose cats than dogs?'
Line the two bars up side by side and count the squares by which the taller bar sticks up above the shorter one
Write the answer as a subtraction, e.g. cats 9 − dogs 6 = 3, and say in words that 3 is 'how many more'

Repeat with a put-together question ('how many chose cats and dogs together?') and a take-apart question ('15 children chose cats or dogs; use the cats bar to find how many of them did NOT choose cats, then check with the dogs bar') to practise combining and separating counts
activities.insight: A comparison answer is the difference between two bars (the gap at the top), not the height of the taller bar; put-together and take-apart questions use the same read-the-scale skill with addition or subtraction.

activities.title: Picture graph with uniform, aligned symbols
steps: Represent the same data as a picture graph, placing exactly one equal-sized symbol per unit in each category's row
Align symbols in rows so the length of a row can be compared at a glance

Read a category's count by counting its symbols, and answer a 'how many more' question by lining up the two rows and counting only the EXTRA symbols in the longer row (the difference, not the longer row's total)
Discuss what goes wrong if symbols are different sizes or not lined up
activities.insight: Symbols must be uniform and aligned so that a row's length faithfully represents its count; 'how many more' is still the difference between the two counts, read as the extra symbols in the longer row.

activities.title: Check questions: read, compare, and construct
steps: Answer a 'how many more' multiple-choice or short-answer item where one tempting wrong answer is the taller bar's raw value
Set bar heights (by drawing or dragging a slider) to match given counts, keeping equal width and a zero baseline
Explain in one sentence how you found a difference, so the reasoning (subtraction vs. height) is visible
Answer a scale-awareness prompt: 'if the dogs bar started halfway up, would it still tell us 6? why not?'
activities.insight: Fluency means reading values against the scale, computing comparisons as differences, and constructing well-formed bars — all three, not just recognising a correct graph.

checkQuestion: First: here is a bar graph of our class's favourite pets — how many MORE children chose cats than dogs, and how do you know? Then: here is the data for fish (4) and birds (2) — add those two bars to the graph correctly.
checkAnswer: Interpreting: reads both bars against the scale and gives the DIFFERENCE (e.g. cats 9 − dogs 6 = 3), explaining the comparison. Translating: draws a fish bar to 4 and a birds bar to 2, equal width, rising from the baseline, correctly against the scale.
